column3: It explicitly says Pharaoh's people followed his command and that his command was not rightly directed.
Pharaoh's arrogant self-exaltation with his forces supplies the character setting for his failed leadership.
It contrasts a group's attempt to lead others astray with the focus ayah's successful misdirection of a people.
Pharaoh's challenge to the Lordship of the worlds exposes the false theological stance behind his leadership.
God gives Musa a safe route for the servants, directly opposing Pharaoh's destructive pursuit of his people.
Its opposition of divine guidance and being led astray frames the two outcomes named in the focus ayah.
The bare mention of Pharaoh identifies the same figure but adds no account of his leading.
The preceding ayah shows Pharaoh leading his forces in pursuit into the sea, whose outcome the focus ayah assesses.
The inability to guide people away from their error offers a relevant contrast to Pharaoh's failure to guide his people.
It shows Pharaoh's oppressive power over his people, explaining why his followers were vulnerable to his direction.
The destruction of Pharaoh and his forces in the sea confirms the ruinous outcome of his leadership.
The brothers' mistaken accusation that their father is astray concerns neither Pharaoh nor leadership of a people.
Pharaoh publicly appeals to his people through claims of power and possession, a direct instance of his manipulative leadership.
Musa and Harun are sent with signs, establishing the divine counter-mission to Pharaoh's direction of his people.
Following desire without knowledge and being beyond guidance provides a general model for the error attributed to Pharaoh's people.
The loss of disbelievers' deeds concerns misdirection in outcome, without a leader-follower relation.
It sets guidance and manifest error in contrast, the evaluative distinction made about Pharaoh's leadership.
God's not guiding wrongdoers parallels the focus ayah's verdict that Pharaoh did not guide his people.
It states that God guides and lets stray after messengers clarify matters, framing guidance as distinct from Pharaoh's human direction.
The destruction of earlier peoples is presented as guidance through signs, contrasting Pharaoh's failure to lead his people rightly.
The Quran as guidance for believers gives only a broad positive counterpart to Pharaoh's lack of guidance.
The response of Lot's people to the righteous does not clarify Pharaoh's leadership or misguidance.
Separate liability for each side's deeds only loosely relates to the consequences of following a leader.
God's knowledge of who has strayed and who is guided directly frames the two states in the focus ayah.
Persistent blindness and greater straying describe the condition to which bad direction can lead.
The gathering of criminals on the Last Day has no focused connection to Pharaoh leading his people astray.
Calling dispute about the Hour distant error is a general use of straying, not a leadership relation.
The worse path and destination of the condemned reflects misguidance's result but not Pharaoh's role.
The sea-destruction of Pharaoh and his forces confirms the fatal end of the leadership described in the focus ayah.
Some descendants are guided while many are defiantly disobedient, offering only a general community-level contrast.
The absence of a heavenly army after a believer's death does not bear on Pharaoh's guidance of his people.
Musa's call at the sacred valley is not about Pharaoh's direction of his people.
The security and guidance of uncorrupted believers provide a broad positive contrast only.
Following desire rather than God's guidance closely describes the kind of misdirection embodied by Pharaoh's rule.
Following a false patron results in being led astray and directed toward fire, a close leader-follower parallel.
God's refusal to guide defiantly corrupt people parallels the stated absence of guidance under Pharaoh.
Its description of people farther from the right path is general and does not concern Pharaoh's leadership.
Musa is commanded to leave with God's servants because they will be pursued, setting up Pharaoh's harmful direction of his forces.
God's knowledge of the straying and the rightly guided supplies the same evaluative contrast as the focus ayah.
Disputing without knowledge, guidance, or illuminating scripture is only a general contrast to sound direction.
The command to follow revealed law rather than ignorant desires offers a normative opposite to Pharaoh's leadership.
God's guidance through clear signs contrasts with Pharaoh's inability to guide his own people.
Guidance and mercy for the doers of good offer only a broad positive counterpart.
A person ruled by desire is left astray and cannot then be guided, closely explaining false direction and its consequence.
Musa identifies Satan as an open misleader within the Pharaoh narrative, providing a relevant source of corrupt direction.
God's guidance distinguishes those who follow the messenger, but the ayah is not about Pharaoh or his people.
The command to leave the sea open because Pharaoh's army will drown gives the narrative consequence of his pursuit.
The Quran's straight guidance provides a clear positive contrast to Pharaoh's failure to guide.
Pharaoh gathers his scheme and comes forward, showing his active mobilization against Musa before the later misguidance verdict.
The extraction of believers from another town does not clarify Pharaoh's leadership.
God guides followers of His approval along paths of peace, a direct positive counter-model to Pharaoh's direction.
The mission to Pharaoh and his elite identifies the resistant ruling group behind the focus narrative.
Personal guidance after being lost is not a leader-to-community case.
Rejecting a warner and declaring the warners astray shows how refusal of guidance produces grave error.
The warnings sent to Pharaoh's people supply the guidance they rejected under his rule.
The protection of infant Musa begins the wider Pharaoh narrative but does not address his leadership of the people.
The qualities of those hoped to be guided are only a broad contrast to Pharaoh's people.
Musa is directed to confront Pharaoh's people over their lack of reverence, directly locating the group later misled.
The number of keepers over Hell has no connection to the focus ayah.
A confession of manifest error is relevant only at the level of the word 'astray.'
Pharaoh disobeys the messenger and is severely seized, demonstrating the disastrous course set by rejecting divine direction.
Ships on the sea do not clarify Pharaoh's guidance or misguidance.
A believer's hypothetical error is not about directing a community.
Pharaoh sends mobilizers through the cities, a concrete act of gathering people into his hostile course.
The repeated question about divine favors has no focused link to Pharaoh's leadership.
Guidance to faith is God's favor, contrasting with Pharaoh's false claim to direct his people.
It directly states that the Samiri led Musa's people astray, the closest parallel to Pharaoh misleading his people.
The repeated question about divine favors has no focused link to Pharaoh's leadership.
The Israelites' hope of being guided in identifying the cow does not illuminate Pharaoh's leadership.
The Prophet's freedom from straying is a general opposite, without a community-leadership relationship.
Musa's trust that his Lord will guide him provides a direct contrast to Pharaoh, who did not guide.
Pharaoh's evil deed is made attractive and he is barred from the way, directly exposing the falsity of his claimed direction.
Pharaoh claims to guide his people only to the way of right conduct, directly contradicted by the focus ayah's verdict.
The destruction of what Pharaoh and his people built records the collapse of their shared oppressive order.
Clear insights, guidance, and mercy for a convinced people offer only a general positive contrast.
A people's false accusation that their prophet is astray has no specific link to Pharaoh's leading.
Giving Musa the Book and criterion so his people may be guided supplies the divine alternative to Pharaoh's misdirection.
The mention of Abraham's and Lot's peoples does not clarify the focus ayah.
It distinguishes a person's own guidance from another's straying, qualifying the responsibility of Pharaoh's followers.
Those whom God lets stray have no guide and wander in excess, a broad account of uncorrected misdirection.
God's ongoing guidance is a direct positive contrast to Pharaoh's inability to guide his people.
The elite warn their people not to follow Shu'ayb, a close pattern of leaders steering a community away from guidance.
The Creator alone will guide, countering Pharaoh's pretension to direct his people.
A community elite labels its prophet foolish and lying, but this does not itself describe leading the people astray.
It denies that anyone can guide one whom God has let stray, framing the focus ayah's failed guidance in divine terms.
Noah's elite disparage his followers, with only an indirect resemblance to corrupt community leadership.
Following ancestors found astray shows how a community can inherit and continue misdirection.
Musa speaks of God guiding and letting stray amid a trial of his people, a relevant communal counterpart.
Remembering God for having guided former strayers is only a broad contrast.
It states that guidance and straying return upon the individual, clarifying the followers' accountability under Pharaoh.
People's refusal to humble themselves after punishment does not address Pharaoh's leadership.
Musa contrasts the one who brings divine guidance with wrongdoers, directly relevant in his dispute with Pharaoh.
The oath by the night and what it gathers has no connection to the focus ayah.
Musa's people recognize that they have gone astray and seek mercy, a communal example of acknowledged misdirection.
The oath by the soul and its proportioning does not clarify Pharaoh's leadership.
God's showing of the two paths provides the positive alternative to being led astray.
The Prophet's sanity is unrelated to Pharaoh's guidance of his people.
The eventual exposure of those extended in error mentions misguidance and weak forces but no direct Pharaoh link.
A prayer for forgiveness, steadfastness, and victory does not address Pharaoh's leadership.
Musa offers to guide Pharaoh to his Lord, directly contrasting God's offered guidance with Pharaoh's later misguidance.
Israel's rescue from Pharaoh's people, who subjected them to severe torment, shows the oppressive communal order from which Pharaoh's leadership had to be escaped.
The sea's division for Israel and drowning of Pharaoh's people gives the decisive consequence of the course Pharaoh led them upon.
Musa's mission to Pharaoh and his chiefs with signs establishes the direct narrative setting for Pharaoh's later misguidance of his people.
Pharaoh's coercive response to the believing magicians displays the authoritarian control through which he held his people to his course.
Pharaoh's chiefs urge him to leave Musa to spread corruption and abandon Pharaoh's gods, exposing the ruler-centered religion that competes with divine guidance.
The oppressed people complain that Pharaoh harmed them before and after Musa came, directly showing their condition under his rule.
The affliction of Pharaoh's people is a warning intended to recall them, in contrast with their continuing attachment to his order.
Pharaoh's people attribute misfortune to Musa and his followers, illustrating their distorted judgment under the ruling conflict.
The drowning of Pharaoh and his people records the final outcome of their collective denial and pursuit.
Musa and Harun are sent with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, establishing the prophetic alternative to their leadership.
Musa says Pharaoh and his chiefs have been given wealth so that they lead people astray from God's way, directly paralleling the focus ayah.
Pharaoh's pursuit of the Children of Israel in rebellion and hostility culminates the destructive direction attributed to him.
Musa's mission to Pharaoh and his chiefs with signs gives the immediate setting for the following judgment on Pharaoh's command.
Pharaoh will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire, the clearest explicit parallel to his leading them astray.
The curse following Pharaoh and his people in this world and the next confirms the lasting result of their shared course.
Pharaoh's rejection of Musa's nine clear signs shows his refusal of the guidance offered to him and his people.
Musa identifies Pharaoh as doomed despite the signs, explaining why Pharaoh cannot be a sound guide for his people.
God commands Musa to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, naming the moral condition behind his misguiding rule.
Musa and Harun are sent together to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, reinforcing the direct divine challenge to his leadership.
Musa and Harun warn Pharaoh not to transgress, setting divine guidance against Pharaoh's oppressive course.
God reminds the Children of Israel that He saved them from their enemy, identifying Pharaoh's rule as the danger from which they were delivered.
Harun tells the people that the Samiri has led them astray, an explicit intra-surah parallel to Pharaoh leading his people astray.
The promise that following God's guidance prevents straying offers the direct theological opposite of Pharaoh's failed guidance.
Musa is commanded to go to Pharaoh because he is a transgressing people, establishing the confrontation with corrupt rule.
Musa and Harun identify themselves to Pharaoh as messengers of the Lord of the worlds, confronting his false authority.
Pharaoh's threat to punish the magicians after their belief shows how he tried to control public allegiance against guidance.
God commands Musa to depart with His servants, because Pharaoh's forces will pursue them under his direction.
Pharaoh publicly characterizes the Israelites to mobilize his people against them, an explicit act of directing communal hostility.
The parted sea provides the divinely guided route for Musa's people, directly opposing Pharaoh's destructive pursuit.
The drowning of the others concludes the course Pharaoh led against the divinely guided escape.
The account of Musa and Pharaoh is introduced as truth for believers, framing the focus ayah within its wider leadership narrative.
Pharaoh exalts himself, divides the people into factions, and oppresses one faction, directly describing the social machinery of his rule.
Pharaoh's claim that his people have no god but him exposes the false religious authority by which he misdirects them.
God says that Pharaoh and his party were made leaders calling to the Fire, directly defining the destination of their leadership.
Pharaoh and his party are followed by a curse in this world and are among the despised on the Day of Resurrection, confirming their ruinous guidance.
Musa is sent to Pharaoh, Haman, and Qarun with signs and clear authority, establishing the divine challenge to Pharaoh's court.
The naming of Pharaoh, Haman, and Qarun as recipients of Musa's mission identifies the ruling coalition opposing guidance.
Pharaoh orders the killing of the sons of those who believe with Musa, showing the coercion used to preserve his people's allegiance.
The believing man from Pharaoh's family warns against killing Musa, an internal challenge to Pharaoh's destructive rule.
The believing man addresses Pharaoh's people and warns them of a day like that of earlier factions, countering Pharaoh's direction before its ruinous outcome.
The believing man tells Pharaoh's people to follow him and promises to guide them to the way of right conduct, explicitly contrasting Pharaoh's false claim to guide them.
God protects the believing man from Pharaoh's evil and surrounds Pharaoh's people with punishment, confirming the danger of their ruler's course.
Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire and commanded into its harshest punishment, giving the final destination of the people he led.
Musa is sent with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, setting the narrative of Pharaoh's public influence over his people.
Pharaoh swayed his people and they obeyed him, the most explicit statement of his successful manipulation of them.
When Pharaoh's people provoked divine wrath, they were drowned together, showing the consequence of their obedience to him.
The trial of Pharaoh's people through a noble messenger establishes that they received guidance before rejecting it.
The Israelites were saved from Pharaoh, described as an arrogant transgressor, reinforcing the character judgment behind his failed leadership.
Musa's mission to Pharaoh with clear authority supplies another direct framing of the prophetic challenge to him.
Pharaoh's people denied all the warnings, explaining why neither the signs nor their ruler's course yielded sound guidance.
Pharaoh's wife prays for rescue from Pharaoh and his deeds, an internal testimony to the evil of his rule.
The Messenger is compared to the messenger sent to Pharaoh, linking Pharaoh's rejection of divine guidance with the warning to later communities.
Pharaoh's claim, 'I am your highest lord,' exposes the false sovereignty that makes his direction of the people fundamentally corrupt.
God's exemplary punishment of Pharaoh confirms the outcome of his arrogant claim and rejection of guidance.
